title: Taurine hypomodification underlies mitochondrial tRNA Trp -related genetic diseases

sections.abstract: E scherichia c oli MnmE and MnmG form a complex ( Ec MnmEG), generating transfer RNA (tRNA) 5-carboxymethylaminomethyluridine (cmnm 5 U) modification. Both cmnm 5 U and equivalent 5-taurinomethyluridine (τm 5 U, catalyzed by homologous GTPBP3 and MTO1) are found at U34 in several human mitochondrial tRNAs (hmtRNAs). Certain mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations, including m.3243A > G in tRNA Leu (UUR) and m.8344A > G in tRNA Lys , cause genetic diseases, partially due to τm 5 U hypomodification. However, whether other mtDNA variants in different tRNAs cause a defect in τm 5 U biogenesis remains unknown. Here, we purified naturally assembled Ec MnmEG from E. coli . Notably, Ec MnmEG was able to incorporate both cmnm 5 U and τm 5 U into hmtRNA Trp (encoded by MT-TW ), providing a valuable basis for directly monitoring the effects of mtDNA mutations on U34 modification. In vitro , several clinical hmtRNA Trp pathogenic mutations caused U34 hypomodification. A patient harboring an m.5541C > T mutation exhibited hmtRNA Trp τm 5 U hypomodification. Moreover, using mtDNA base editing, we constructed two cell lines carrying m.5532G > A or m.5545C > T mutations, both of which exhibited hmtRNA Trp τm 5 U hypomodification. Taurine supplementation improved mitochondrial translation in patient cells. Our findings describe the third hmtRNA species with mutation-related τm 5 U-hypomodification and provide new insights into the pathogenesis and intervention strategy for hmtRNA Trp -related genetic diseases.
sections.introduction:
Over 170 types of RNA modifications have been identified in various RNAs across all domains of life ( 1 ). Notably, transfer RNAs (tRNAs) are the most extensively modified RNA species in cells, accounting for approximately 80% of the modification types. Most tRNA modifications are located in the anticodon loop, stabilizing codon–anticodon interactions and extending or restricting the decoding capability of a given tRNA during translation ( 2 , 3 ). For example, 5-carboxymethylaminomethyluridine (cmnm 5 U) ( Supplementary Figure S1A ) is found at position 34 of tRNAs in bacteria, eukaryotic mitochondria and archaea ( 4–6 ). cmnm 5 U strengthens the recognition of purine-ending codons and prevents the misrecognition of near-cognate codons ending in pyrimidines ( 2 , 7 ), which is crucial for efficient and accurate mRNA translation.

In Escherichia coli , MnmE ( Ec MnmE) and MnmG ( Ec MnmG) are evolutionarily conserved tRNA-modifying enzymes that form an α 2 β 2 heterotetrameric complex (designated hereafter as Ec MnmEG) to jointly catalyze cmnm 5 U formation in six E. coli tRNAs— Ec tRNA Lys (UUU), Ec tRNA Glu (UUC), Ec tRNA Gln (UUG), Ec tRNA Leu (UAA), Ec tRNA Arg (UCU) and Ec tRNA Gly (UCC)—using glycine (Gly), 5,10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate (5,10-CH 2 -THF), flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH) and guanosine triphosphate (GTP) as substrates ( 1 , 8 , 9 ). A series of cmnm 5 U derivatives have been found among some of these Ec tRNAs ( 1 ).

In mammalian cells, 5-taurinomethyluridine (τm 5 U) and 5-taurinomethyl-2-thiouridine (τm 5 s 2 U) ( Supplementary Figure S1B ) are structurally equivalent to cmnm 5 U and 5-carboxymethylaminomethyl-2-thiouridine (cmnm 5 s 2 U) ( Supplementary Figure S1A ), respectively, in which the Gly moiety is replaced with taurine. Their incorporation is achieved by GTPBP3 and MTO1, which are homologs of Ec MnmE and Ec MnmG, respectively ( Supplementary Figures S2 and S3 ) ( 10–13 ). τm 5 U is present in two human mitochondrial tRNAs (hmtRNAs), namely hmtRNA Leu (UUR) (encoded by MT-TL1 ) and hmtRNA Trp (encoded by MT-TW ), while the τm 5 s 2 U modification predominates in hmtRNA Lys (encoded by MT-TK ), hmtRNA Gln (encoded by MT-TQ ) and hmtRNA Glu (encoded by MT-TE ) along with a small amount of τm 5 U ( 6 , 11 ). Interestingly, under physiological or taurine-starvation conditions, both cmnm 5 U and cmnm 5 s 2 U are detected in hmtRNAs ( 6 , 11 ), suggesting the plasticity of human modification enzymes.

Modification of τm 5 U stabilizes U:G wobble pairing to promote accurate decoding of purine-ending codons ( 14 , 15 ). Given their crucial role in codon decoding, gene mutations in both human GTPBP3 (h GTPBP3 ) and MTO1 (h MTO1 ) lead to mitochondrial diseases, with the most common clinical manifestations being lactic acidosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy ( 16 , 17 ). Mto1 -deficient mice exhibit τm 5 U modification deficiency ( 18 ) and myocardial damage caused by mitochondrial dysfunction ( 19 ). Deletion of h GTPBP3 in human cell lines results in mitochondrial translation deficiency ( 11 ). Deletion of GTPBP3 or MTO1 in zebrafish leads to aberrant mitochondrial tRNA metabolism and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy ( 20 , 21 ). Our previous study revealed that various pathogenic mutations in hGTPBP3 severely reduce GTPase activity and alter steady-state levels, structure and function of the protein in vitro and in vivo ( 22 ).

Numerous maternally inherited mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) variants are associated with various human diseases with different symptoms. For example, m.3243A > G mutation in hmtRNA Leu (UUR) and m.8344A > G mutation in hmtRNA Lys lead to τm 5 U hypomodification and inability to efficiently decode the cognate codons ( 14 , 23 ), thus causing mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes (MELAS) and myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers (MERRF), respectively ( 24–27 ). However, the underlying molecular basis for τm 5 U modification defects induced by both m.3243A > G and m.8344A > G mutations is unknown. Among the clinically reported pathogenic mutations, there are also other variants on hmtRNA Leu (UUR) associated with τm 5 U modification defect, including G3244A, T3258A, T3271C and T3291C ( 28 ), located in the T-loop, anticodon stem and D-loop, respectively. Patients harboring other hmtRNA Leu (UUR) mutations without a MELAS phenotype exhibit a normal τm 5 U level ( 28 ). Besides hmtRNA Leu (UUR) and hmtRNA Lys , many pathogenic mutations on the other three τm 5 (s 2 )U-harboring hmtRNAs, including hmtRNA Trp , are associated with human diseases ( http://www.mitomap.org ) ( 29–31 ). However, whether these variants in other hmtRNAs lead to τm 5 U modification defects remains an open question.

Despite extensive efforts, we failed to purify mature hMTO1 from the E. coli expression system due to protein aggregation. Moreover, in vitro τm 5 U modification efficiency using purified hGTPBP3–hMTO1 complex from human cells is quite low (approximately 3.3%) ( 11 ). Thus, it is difficult to reveal the molecular basis of τm 5 U modification defect induced by hmtRNA, hGTPBP3 or hMTO1 mutations using a native or reconstituted hGTPBP3–hMTO1 complex. Given this limitation, we aimed to explore the potential cross-recognition of hmtRNAs by the Ec MnmEG, which could provide insight into the molecular pathogenesis of human τm 5 U-related diseases due to mtDNA variants.

To this end, we purified a naturally assembled Ec MnmEG complex, which is active in mediating tRNA modification. Using the tRNA substrate plasticity of the Ec MnmEG, we demonstrated that mtDNA mutations in the anticodon stem and loop regions of hmtRNA Trp impair U34 modification in vitro . Furthermore, by using a patient-derived cybrid cell line and two mtDNA-edited cell lines, we verified that selected mutations in the anticodon and D-stem of the hmtRNA Trp locus abolish τm 5 U biogenesis in vivo . Finally, we demonstrated that taurine supplementation is a promising approach for improving mitochondrial translation impaired by pathogenic hmtRNA Trp mutations. Our results provide the third example of an hmtRNA species exhibiting mutation-related τm 5 U hypomodification and shed light into pathogenesis and intervention of specific mtDNA variants.
sections.methods:
T4 DNA ligase, Lipo8000 transfection reagent and penicillin–streptomycin were purchased from Beyotime Biotechnology (Shanghai, China). Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM) was purchased from Corning (New York, NY, USA). Fetal bovine serum (FBS) was purchased from ExCell Bio (Guangzhou, China). Sodium pyruvate was obtained from Gibco (Carlsbad, CA, USA). Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes and benzonase were purchased from Merck (Darmstadt, Germany). Ni 2+ -NTA Superflow resin was purchased from QIAGEN, Inc. (Hilden, Germany). The FAD, NADH, anti-digoxigenin-AP and CDP-star antibodies were purchased from Roche (Basel, Switzerland). Tris-HCl, A/U/C/GTP, Gly, taurine, isopropyl-d-thiogalactoside (IPTG), digitonin, maleic acid, mannitol, sucrose, ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), l-glutamine, d-glucose, pyruvate, Bis-Tris, 6-aminohexanoic acid and G250 were purchased from Sangon Biotech (Shanghai, China), while 5,10-CH 2 -THF was obtained from Schirmer Laboratories (Rapperswil-Jona, Switzerland). A protein inhibitor cocktail, uridine, phosphodiesterase, sodium acetate and streptavidin agarose beads were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). The PrimeScript RT Master Mix and PrimerSTAR Max DNA Polymerase were purchased from TaKaRa Bio (Kyoto, Japan). Restriction endonucleases and bacterial alkaline phosphatase were purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific (Waltham, MA, USA). TRIzol Universal was purchased from Tiangen Biotech (Beijing, China). The KOD-Plus Kit was purchased from TOYOBO (Osaka, Japan). Protein Ladder, primer synthesis and DNA sequencing were purchased and performed by Tsingke (Shanghai, China). Dig- and biotin-labelled primers were synthesized by Biosune (Shanghai, China). The T4 polynucleotide kinase was obtained from Vazyme Biotechnology (Nanjing, China). The competent E. coli BL21 (DE3) cells were purchased from Weidi Biotechnology (Shanghai, China). [ 3 H]Gly and [ 14 C]taurine were obtained from Perkin Elmer Inc. (Waltham, MA, USA). cmnm 5 U and τm 5 U standard samples were obtained from Biosynth Carbosynth (Switzerland) and Alsachim (France), respectively.

The following antibodies were used in this study: rabbit anti-TOMM40 (18409–1-AP; Proteintech, Rosemont. Il, USA), rabbit anti-MT-ND2 (A6180; ABclonal Technology, Woburn, MA, USA), rabbit anti-MT-ND3 (A9940; ABclonal Technology), rabbit anti-MT-ND4 (A9941; ABclonal Technology), rabbit anti-MT-ND5 (A17972; ABclonal Technology), rabbit anti-MT-ND6 (A17991; ABclonal Technology), rabbit anti-NDUFS1 (12444–1-AP; Proteintech), rabbit anti-SDHB (10620–1-AP; Proteintech), rabbit anti-MT-COX2 (55070–1-AP; Proteintech), rabbit anti-COX4 (11242–1-AP; Proteintech), rabbit anti-MT-ATP6 (A8193; ABclonal Technology), rabbit anti-MT-ATP8 (A17890; ABclonal Technology), rabbit anti-GTPBP3 (custom-made, ABclonal Technology), rabbit anti-MTO1 (PA5-98720; Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA), mouse anti-His 6 (012HS01; AbHO), mouse anti-FLAG (66008-3-Ig; Proteintech), mouse anti-GAPDH (60004-1-Ig; Proteintech), goat anti-mouse IgG (A21010; Abbkine, Wuhan, China) and goat anti-rabbit IgG (A21020; Abbkine).

The genes encoding Ec MnmE (No. P25522 ; UniProt, Geneva, Switzerland) and Ec MnmG (No. P0A6U3 , UniProt) were amplified from the E. coli K-12 MG1655 genome and separately inserted into multiple cloning sites 1 (between the NcoI and NotI sites) and 2 (between the NdeI and XhoI sites) of pETDuet-1 to obtain pETDuet- Ec MnmE-His 6 - Ec MnmG-FLAG. The construct was transfected into E. coli BL21 (DE3) cells. When the cells reached an optical density at 600 nm ( A 600 ) of 0.8, gene expression was induced with a final concentration of 400 μM IPTG at 18°C for 10 h. The primers used for cloning are listed in Supplementary Table S1 .

Escherichia coli cells were lysed by sonication in lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 300 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 10 mM imidazole and then centrifuged at 47 850 g at 4°C for 1 h. The supernatant was incubated with Ni 2+ -NTA Superflow resin at 4°C for 45 min, washed with 80 ml lysis buffer supplemented with 20 mM imidazole and finally eluted in lysis buffer supplemented with 250 mM imidazole. The eluted protein Ec MnmEG was concentrated and then applied to a Superdex 200 column with 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.5), 50 mM NaCl, 100 mM KCl, 5 mM MgCl 2 , 5 mM β-mercaptoethanol. The fractions were collected for sodiumdodecyl sulphate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS–PAGE) analysis, and certain fractions were concentrated for subsequent experiments. All proteins were stored at −20°C after mixing with an equal volume of glycerol. Protein concentrations were determined using a protein quantification kit (BCA Assay; Beyotime). To determine molecular weight (MW), protein standards were loaded onto Superdex 200 under the same conditions. A linear calibration curve was obtained by plotting the logarithms of the known MWs of the standards versus their elution times.

The constructs encoding hmtRNA Leu (UUR), hmtRNA Lys (a Ki mutant for correct folding) ( 32 ) and hmtRNA Trp have been described in previous reports ( 33–35 ). The gene encoding hmtRNA Gln with an upstream T7 promoter was inserted into the pUC19 plasmid. The genes encoding hmtRNA Glu , Ec tRNA Lys (UUU), Ec tRNA Leu (UAA), Ec tRNA Gln (UUG), Ec RNA Gly (UCC), Ec tRNA Arg (UCU), Ec tRNA Glu (UUC) with an upstream T7 promoter were incorporated into the pTrc99b plasmid between the EcoRI and BamHI sites. tRNA gene mutagenesis was performed according to the protocol provided with the KOD-plus mutagenesis kit. All tRNAs were obtained using in vitro T7 RNA polymerase transcription as previously described ( 36 ). The primers used for template preparation are listed in Supplementary Table S1 .

The cmnm 5 U modification reaction was performed at 37°C in a 40 μl reaction mixture containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.5), 100 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl 2 , 10 mM GTP, 2.5 mM FAD, 2.5 mM NADH, 2.5 mM 5,10-CH 2 -THF, 5 mM dithiothreitol (DTT), 20 μM [ 3 H]Gly, 10 μM Ec tRNAs or hmtRNAs and 2 μM Ec MnmEG. The τm 5 U modification reaction was performed at 37°C in a 40 μl reaction mixture containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.5), 100 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl 2 , 10 mM GTP, 2.5 mM FAD, 2.5 mM NADH, 2.5 mM 5,10-CH 2 -THF, 5 mM DTT, 50 μM [ 14 C]taurine, 10 μM Ec tRNAs or hmtRNAs and 2 μM Ec MnmEG. Aliquots of 9 μl of reaction solution were taken at specific time points and quenched on Whatman filter pads. Samples were processed as described previously ( 36 ).

For the preparation of cmnm 5 U-modified Ec tRNA Arg (UCU) or hmtRNA Trp , the reaction was performed in a 200 μl mixture containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.5), 100 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl 2 , 5 mM DTT, 10 mM GTP, 2.5 mM FAD, 2.5 mM NADH, 2.5 mM 5,10-CH 2 -THF, 2 mM Gly, 5 μM Ec MnmEG and 50–100 ng tRNA transcripts. For the preparation of τm 5 U-modified hmtRNA Trp , the reaction was performed in a 200 μl mixture containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.5), 100 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl 2 , 5 mM DTT, 10 mM GTP, 2.5 mM FAD, 2.5 mM NADH, 2.5 mM 5,10-CH 2 -THF, 5 mM taurine, 5 μM Ec MnmEG and 50–100 ng hmtRNA Trp . All reaction mixtures were incubated at 37°C for 1 h, then purified by phenol/chloroform and precipitated by EtOH with NaOAc overnight at −20°C. Concentrations were determined by denaturing urea-PAGE based on the linear curves from samples of tRNA transcripts of known concentrations.

Five hundred nanograms of tRNA transcripts or cmnm 5 U- and τm 5 U-modified tRNAs were digested with 10 U/ml benzonase, 0.5 U/ml bacterial alkaline phosphatase and 10 mg/ml phosphodiesterase supplied with 100 mM NaOAc (pH 5.2) at 37°C for 2 days. After filtration, 20 μl of the product were subjected to ultra-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS). The mononucleosides were separated by high performance liquid chromatography on a Zorbax Eclipse Plus C18 column (2.1 50 and 1.8 mm; Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA) and detected using a model 6495 QQQ triple-quadrupole mass spectrometer (Agilent Technologies) in the positive ion multiple reaction-monitoring mode. Mass transitions from m/z 332.9 to 124.9 (cmnm 5 U) and m/z 382.1 to 125.1 (τm 5 U) were monitored and recorded with Poroshell 120 PFP column (Agilent Technologies).

Q Exactive™ Plus Orbitrap mass spectrometer equipped with an electrospray ionization (ESI) source and a DNA Pac RP column (100 × 2.1 mm, 4 μm) (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for both tRNA molecular mass determination and fragment analysis. Liquid chromatography (LC) solvent system consisted of 2% 1,1,1,3,3,3-Hexafluoroisopropanol (HFIP) and 0.1% tetraethylammonium in H 2 O (solvent A) and methanol (solvent B). For tRNA molecular mass determination, the samples were separated at a flow rate of 300 μl/min using a linear gradient of 5% B in 0–2 min, 5–90% B in 2–5 min, 90% B in 5–6 min, 90–5% B in 0.1 min and 5% B in 6.1–10 min. Full mass spectrometry (MS) scan range was set to 600–3000 m/z in negative mode, Automatic Gain Control (AGC) 100% and Max IT 100 ms. The ESI source parameters were set as follows: spray voltage 3.3 kV; sheath gas 40 arbitrary unit (Arb); aux gas 10 Arb; ion transfer tube temp 320°C; vaporizer temp 350°C; rheumatoidfactor lens 70. For fragment mapping, different tRNA samples [including cmnm 5 U- Ec tRNA Arg (UCU) and cmnm 5 U-, τm 5 U-hmtRNA Trp ] (5 μg) were incubated with 1 μl RNase T1 and 44 μl SMART digest RNase Buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 37°C for 5–30 min, respectively. After digestion, the mixture was diluted with one-tenth volume of 0.1 M triethylamine acetate (pH 7.0), and 2 μl was used for LC-MS analysis. The samples were separated at a flow rate of 300 μl/min using a linear gradient of 1% B in 0–2 min, 1–30% B in 2–15 min, 30–90% B in 15–16 min, 90–1% B in 0.1 min and 1% B in 16.1–20 min. The ESI source parameters were the same as above. Additionally, the High energy Collision Dissociation (HCD) was performed by data-dependent scan with collision energy 21, 23 and 25. Biopharma Finder and Xcalicur (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were used for data analysis.

For determination of steady-state tRNA level, 3 μg of total RNA was loaded on a 10% PAGE-8 M urea gel and then transferred to nylon membranes. After ultraviolet crosslinking, the membranes were blocked in prehybridization solution supplementary with saline sodium citrate buffer (SSC) solution containing 0.6 M NaCl and 60 mM sodium citrate, 20 mM Na 2 HPO 4 , 7% SDS, Denhardt solution and 0.4 mg / l fish sperm DNA at 55°C for 1 h and then hybridized with Dig-labelled probes ( Supplementary Table S2 ) at 55°C overnight. The membranes were washed with washing buffer containing 0.1 M maleic acid, 0.15 M NaCl (pH 7.5) and 0.3% Tween-20 and then incubated with anti-digoxigenin-AP buffer for 1.5 h. After washing twice with phosphate-buffered saline-Tween (PBST), the membranes were treated with CDP-star and examined using a chemiluminescence assay.

Mitochondria were isolated as previously described ( 37 ). Briefly, the cells were digested and washed three times with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). The cells were then disrupted in a solution supplemented with 225 mM mannitol, 76 mM sucrose, 30 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5) and 0.075 mM EDTA (pH 8.0) for 15 min, using an ice-cold ULTRA-TURRAX Disperser (IKE). The homogenate was centrifuged twice at 600 g for 5 min at 4°C and the supernatant was transferred to 1.5 ml tubes and centrifuged twice at 7000 g for 5 min at 4°C. The mitochondria pellet was stored at -80°C.

Cells or mitochondria were lysed with lysis buffer containing 20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 0.1% SDS and 0.5% sodium deoxycholate plus a protease inhibitor cocktail, and then collected by centrifugation at 13 800 g at 4°C. The proteins were separated by 10% SDS-PAGE and transferred to a PVDF membrane. Blocked by 5% milk for 1 h, the membranes were incubated with indicated primary antibodies at 4°C overnight, and then the secondary antibodies were incubated for 1 h at room temperature. The target bands were detected using chemiluminescence.

Cells were seeded at a density of 2 × 10 4 cells per well on Seahorse XF24 cell culture plates in cell culture medium. The plates were then washed with the XF Assay Medium containing DMEM, 1.85 g/l NaCl, 2 mM l-glutamine, 10 mM d-glucose and 1 mM pyruvate. The oxygen consumption rate (OCR) was determined under sequential additions of 1 μM oligomycin, 1.5 μM carbonyl cyanide 4-(trifluoromethoxy)phenylhydrazone (FCCP), 1 μM rotenone and 1 μM antimycin A. OCR was performed using a model XFe24 instrument (Seahorse Bioscience, North Billerica, MA, USA). After the experiments, cell counts were calculated using Ensight (Revvity) with the dyes propidium iodide (PI) and Hoechst at a 1:1000 dilution.

Mitochondrial proteins were prepared as described above, and their concentrations were determined using a Bradford Protein Assay Kit (P0006; Beyotime). Every 500 μg of the mitochondria was resuspended by 50 μl solubilization buffer A containing 50 mM sodium chloride, 100 mM Bis-Tris and 2 mM 6-aminohexanoic acid. Fifteen microliters of 20% digitonin were added and the mixture was incubated on ice for 10 min. Proteins were collected by centrifugation of the solution at 13 800 g for 10 min at 4°C. The proteins were suspended in 6.25 μl 50% glycerol and 7.5 μl 5% Serva Blue G (SBG) buffer containing 5% G250 and 0.98% aminohexanoic acid. Each sample was loaded on a 3%–12% acrylamide gradient gel and separated by 125 V for 750 min at 4°C. The gel was stained with Coomassie brilliant blue. Further details are provided in previous reference ( 38 ).

tRNA was extracted from wild-type (WT) and mutant cells using the TRIzol reagent (TIANGEN, Beijing, China). Endogenous hmtRNA Trp , hmtRNA Leu (UUR) and hmtRNA Lys were purified by hybridization with biotinylated DNA probes ( Supplementary Table S2 ) using streptavidin agarose resin (20361, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Fifteen microliter of 100 μM DNA probes was incubated with total RNA at 85°C for 5 min and then 37°C for 1.5 h. Streptavidin agarose beads were then added to the incubation mixture for 30 min at room temperature. After washing with PBST three times, the DNA probes were digested by DNase I for 30 min at 37°C. The tRNAs bound to agarose were extracted using TRIzol reagent and precipitated with ethanol. The tRNA purity was confirmed using a urea-PAGE gel.

The DddA-derived cytosine base editor (DdCBE)-targeting plasmids were assembled using the Golden Gate strategy with a previously developed repeat variable di-residue (RVD) library (Shen Lab DdCBE kit, Kit #1000000212) ( 39 ). Briefly, 50 ng of each RVD module and 100 ng of the backbone plasmid underwent digestion and ligation in a single 10 μl reaction containing 0.5 μl of Bsa I (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA, USA) and 0.5 μl of T4 DNA Ligase (New England Biolabs) in T4 DNA ligase buffer. The reaction was subjected to incubation in a thermocycler for 10 cycles of 10 min at 37°C and 10 min at 16°C. Subsequently, the mixture was heated to 50°C for 5 min and then to 80°C for 5 min. Transformation of E. coli competent cells was performed using 2 μl of the ligation mixture. Identification of the assembled plasmids was confirmed by PCR and Sanger sequencing. The PCR and sequencing primers are listed in Supplementary Table S3 . The sequences of the DdCBE plasmids generated in this study are listed in the Supplementary sequence.

HEK293FT cells ( R70007 ; Thermo Fisher Scientific) were cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 3 mM sodium pyruvate and 50 μg/ml uridine at 37°C with 5% CO 2 . Co-transfection of 3 μg of left-DdCBE and 3 μg of right-DdCBE plasmids into cells was performed using the Lonza 4D-Nucleofector with SF Cell Line 4D Nucleofector X Kit. Twenty-four hours post-nucleofection, cells were supplemented with 1 μg/ml puromycin, then collected on Day 3 to detect the editing efficiency by Sanger sequencing and deep sequencing. The cells transfected with the best performance DdCBE pair were harvested to sort individual cells using a FACSAria™ Fusion SORP sorter (BD, Santa Clara, WI, USA) for extended cultivation of single-cell clones.

Genomic DNA was extracted from HEK293FT cells using QuickExtract TM DNA Extraction Solution (Lucigen, Middleton, MA, USA). Fragments spanning the target sites were amplified for Sanger sequencing. Primers used are listed in Supplementary Table S3 . For deep sequencing, the genomic regions of interest were initially amplified with barcoded primers (first-round PCR, PCR1) using Phanta Max Super-Fidelity DNA Polymerase (Vazyme, Nanjing, China). The PCR1 products were pooled with equal moles and purified for the second-round PCR (PCR2). PCR2 was performed using index primers (Vazyme) and purified using clean DNA beads for sequencing on the Illumina NovaSeq platform. The barcoded primers used for PCR1 are listed in Supplementary Table S3 .

For deep-sequencing data analysis, trimmed and filtered reads were aligned to the genome using bowtie2 (v2.3.4.1) with default parameters. The reference sequence for human mtDNA ( NC_012920.1 ) was obtained from the National Center for Biotechnology Information database (NCBI). The BAM and pileup files were converted using samtools (v1.15). The editing frequency of each base was computed using Python and R scripts.
sections.results:
Previously described Ec MnmEG complexes were reconstituted using individually purified subunits ( 8 , 40–43 ). To isolate an intact Ec MnmEG complex, we introduced the genes encoding full-length Ec MnmE with an N-terminal His 6 tag and Ec MnmG with a C-terminal FLAG tag into the dual expression vector pETDuet-1 and expressed them in E. coli . The protein was first purified by Ni-NTA affinity chromatography and then purified by gel filtration chromatography using Superdex 200 (S200). We observed two distinct peaks located at approximately 10.53 and 12.67 ml (Figure 1A ). SDS-PAGE analysis revealed that the first peak at 10.53 ml contained both Ec MnmE and Ec MnmG, whereas the second peak at 12.67 ml predominantly contained Ec MnmE (Figure 1B ). Purified Ec MnmEG complex was further confirmed by Western blot analysis (Figure 1C ). Notably, the purification of Ec MnmG together with Ec MnmE in the first peak suggested a stable interaction between the two proteins in vivo . Based on the high homogeneity and equal molar ratios observed between Ec MnmE and Ec MnmG from 9 to 11 ml gel filtration, we collected and concentrated these fractions for further testing. To assess the quaternary structure of native Ec MnmEG, we applied it to gel filtration analysis on an S200 column. Purified Ec MnmEG was eluted as a single peak (Figure 1D ) corresponding to a calculated MW of 252 kDa, based on the elution volumes of the three standard proteins. Considering that the theoretical MWs of isolated Ec MnmE-His 6 and Ec MnmG-FLAG were 50 and 69 kDa, respectively, this result suggests that purified native Ec MnmEG is an α 2 β 2 heterotetrametric complex in solution, with a theoretical MW of 238 kDa, in agreement with the results of complex reconstitution ( 8 ) and a proposed model obtained with bacterial MnmE and MnmG structures ( 44 , 45 ).

Reconstitution of cmnm 5 U modification in vitro by Ec MnmEG. ( A ) Gel filtration of Ni-NTA purified Ec MnmEG from E. coli on S200. ( B ) SDS-PAGE analysis of elution samples from ( A ) containing Ec MnmEG complex and Ec MnmE . The proteins were stained with Coomassie blue. ( C ) Western blot analyses of purified Ec MnmEG using anti- FLAG and anti-His 6 antibodies. Lane 1: 160 ng, lane 2: 400 ng and lane 3: 800 ng of Ec MnmEG. ( D ) Gel filtration analysis of purified Ec MnmEG on S200 with the elution volumes of standard proteins of known MW indicated, including apoferritin (443 kDa), yeast alcohol dehydrogenase (150 kDa) and bovine serum albumin (66 kDa). ( E ) Time course curves of cmnm 5 U modification of Ec tRNA Lys (UUU), Ec tRNA Leu (UAA), Ec tRNA Gln (UUG), Ec tRNA Gly (UCC), Ec tRNA Arg (UCU) and Ec tRNA Glu (UUC) by Ec MnmEG. Reactions without the addition of tRNA are included as controls. Data represent mean ± SD (standard deviation) ( n = 3). ( F ) UPLC-MS/MS analyses of the digestion product of Ec tRNA Arg (UCU) transcript and cmnm 5 U-modified Ec tRNA Arg (UCU). Mass chromatogram spectra of cmnm 5 U (Q1/Q3 = 332.9/124.9). n.d., not detectable. ( G ) LC-ESI-MS analyses of the cmnm 5 U-modified Ec tRNA Arg (UCU) by Ec MnmEG. Intensity fractions (%) of modified or unmodified fragments are indicated by extracted ion chromatograms. ACCUUCUAAG ( m/z 1591.194) (left) and ACCUcmnm 5 UCUAAG ( m/z 1634.709) (right) for Ec tRNA Arg (UCU). n.d., not detected.

cmnm 5 U modification had been successfully reconstituted on Ec tRNAs by using Gly, 5,10-CH 2 -THF and other cofactors as substrates with Ec MnmEG obtained by incubation of separate MnmE and MnmG ( 40 , 42 , 43 ). To explore whether purified intact Ec MnmEG can catalyze cmnm 5 U formation in vitro , we transcribed its six tRNA substrates, Ec tRNA Lys (UUU), Ec tRNA Glu (UUC), Ec tRNA Gln (UUG), Ec tRNA Leu (UAA), Ec tRNA Arg (UCU) and Ec tRNA Gly (UCC) by in vitro T7 transcription ( Supplementary Figure S4 ). Using [ 3 H]Gly, we found that Ec MnmEG introduced a cmnm 5 U modification in almost all transcripts except Ec tRNA Gln (UUG) (Figure 1E ). The reason for the failure to modify Ec tRNA Gln (UUG) is unclear. It is possible that some modification is a pre-requisite for cmnm 5 U formation in Ec tRNA Gln (UUG). We then confirmed cmnm 5 U modification using UPLC-MS/MS. After digestion of the modified Ec tRNA Arg (UCU) into mononucleosides, UPLC-MS/MS analysis validated that the substrate tRNA was indeed modified with cmnm 5 U in vitro by the Ec MnmEG complex (Figure 1F ). LC-ESI-MS for tRNA fragment analysis of modified Ec tRNA Arg (UCU) suggested the modification site being U34 and revealed modification efficiency being 100% (Figure 1G ). The above data demonstrated that the naturally assembled Ec MnmEG is active in catalyzing tRNA cmnm 5 U modification.

Reconstituting τm 5 U formation in vitro could help in understanding the mechanism of τm 5 U-related diseases, such as MELAS and MERRF. However, the efficiency of τm 5 U modification by the purified hGTPBP3–hMTO1 complex is insufficient to directly examine the effect of pathogenic mutations on τm 5 U formation ( 11 ). We therefore investigated whether τm 5 U could be reconstituted in hmtRNAs by Ec MnmEG, given that the Ec MnmEG complex is a homolog of hGTPBP3–hMTO1 in E. coli .

Considering that Gly is the natural substrate of Ec MnmEG, we first wondered whether hmtRNAs could undergo the cmnm 5 U modification catalyzed by Ec MnmEG. We obtained all five τm 5 (s 2 )U-containing hmtRNA transcripts and detected the cmnm 5 U modification levels of these hmtRNAs by testing the 3 H radioactivity. Remarkably, hmtRNA Trp could be generated with the cmnm 5 U modification, while the other four tRNAs were defective in the cmnm 5 U modification by Ec MnmEG (Figure 2A ). We demonstrated that transcribed hmtRNA Leu (UUR), hmtRNA Trp or hmtRNA Lys (a Ki mutant for folding) ( 32 ) were efficiently aminoacylated by human mitochondrial leucyl-tRNA synthetase ( 33 ), tryptophanyl-tRNA synthetase (hmtTrpRS) ( 35 ) or lysyl-tRNA synthetase ( 34 ), suggesting correct tRNA folding, at least for proper recognition by tRNA synthetases. The modified hmtRNA Trp was collected, digested and analyzed using UPLC-MS/MS. Consistently, cmnm 5 U was readily detected (Figure 2B ). LC-ESI-MS analyses suggested that U34 of hmtRNA Trp was cmnm 5 U-modified with an efficiency of 77.7% (Figure 2C ). These data demonstrated the efficient modification of cmnm 5 U by Ec MnmEG on hmtRNA Trp .

Given the successful incorporation of cmnm 5 U into hmtRNA Trp , we investigated whether Ec MnmEG could modify it with τm 5 U. However, with 50 μM [ 14 C]taurine and hmtRNA Trp as substrates, we failed to detect 14 C radioactivity via liquid scintillation counting. We hypothesized that the binding affinity of Ec MnmEG for taurine might be too low to allow efficient formation of τm 5 U on hmtRNA Trp . Thus, in the presence of 50 μM [ 14 C]taurine, saturation of the enzyme might be too low to allow efficient catalysis. We therefore performed τm 5 U modification of hmtRNA Trp using 5 mM cold taurine. The τm 5 U modification was successfully generated in hmtRNA Trp by Ec MnmEG as determined by UPLC-MS/MS analysis (Figure 2B ). Further LC-ESI-MS analyses revealed that modification efficiency of τm 5 U at position 34 in hmtRNA Trp was 11.5% (Figure 2D ). Thus, Ec MnmEG was able to modify hmtRNA Trp with taurine.

Taken together, these data reveal that Ec MnmEG exhibits a degree of plasticity for tRNA and amino acid substrates. The ability of Ec MnmEG to modify hmtRNA Trp lays a solid foundation for studying the potential molecular pathogenesis of disease-causing mtDNA mutations at the hmtRNA Trp locus.

Efficient incorporation of cmnm 5 U into hmtRNA Trp by Ec MnmEG allows a convenient assessment of the potential effect of mtDNA mutations in hmtRNA Trp on U34 modification using the liquid scintillation method. A broad spectrum of maternally inherited mtDNA mutations at the hmtRNA Trp locus are associated with various human diseases, including mitochondrial myopathy [m.5521G > A ( 46 ), m.5522G > A ( 47 ), m.5532G > A ( 48 ), m.5540G > A ( 49 ), m.5541C > T ( 29 ), m.5543T > C ( 50 )], Leigh syndrome (m.5537_5538insT) ( 51 ), encephalomyopathy (m.5540G > A) ( 49 ), cardiomyopathy (m.5545C > T) ( 52 ) and dementia and chorea (m.5549G > A) ( 53 ) (Figure 3A ). Moreover, a nonpathogenic single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) (m.5563G > A) in the T-loop has been described ( http://mamit-tRNA.u-strasbg.fr ) ( 54 ). All the above pathogenic mutations are concentrated in the D-stem and anticodon stem/loop regions of hmtRNA Trp (Figure 3B ).

We transcribed WT hmtRNA Trp and all of the mutants mentioned above ( Supplementary Figure S5A ). We have previously shown that a natural A29-C41 (m.A5539-m.C5551) mismatch in hmtRNA Trp (Figure 3B ) makes its anticodon stem particularly sensitive to local mutations ( 35 ). Consistently, native PAGE gel analyses of all the hmtRNA Trp transcripts showed that the four mutants in the anticodon stem (m.5537_5538insT, m.5540G > A, m.5541C > T and m.5549G > A) exhibited a slower migration rate ( Supplementary Figure S5B ), suggesting that these mutants exhibited a disrupted anticodon stem, due to the A29-C41 mismatch. We also showed that both the WT hmtRNA Trp and the m.5540G > A mutant (G30A mutant) were efficiently charged by hmtTrpRS, suggesting that aminoacylation by hmtTrpRS is independent of the local structure in the anticodon stem ( 35 ). Moreover, other mutants (m.5521G > A, m.5522G > A, m.5532G > A, m.5543T > C and m.5545C > T) showed migration rate comparable to those of WT hmtRNA Trp , indicating that the three-dimensional structures of these mutants are correctly folded. In vitro modification assays showed that Ec MnmEG only weakly modified the m.5541C > T and m.5545C > T mutants, while all other pathogenic mutations were completely unmodified. In contrast, the modification efficiency of the m.5563G > A mutant was only slightly lower than that of the WT hmtRNA Trp transcript (Figure 3C ).

These results showed that all mutations found in the D-stem, anticodon stem and loop regions of hmtRNA Trp reduce cmnm 5 U34 modification efficiency, as shown by our in vitro Ec MnmEG activity assay.

The defect in cmnm 5 U modification by Ec MnmEG observed in vitro with pathogenic mutations suggests that same hmtRNA Trp mutations could impair τm 5 U modification in vivo . To reveal the effects of hmtRNA Trp mutations on τm 5 U modification status in vivo , we employed our previously established cybrid cell line displaying over 95% mutant mtDNA. This line was generated through mitochondria-mediated transformation of mtDNA-less ρ° cells, using platelets from a MELAS patient carrying m.5541C > T mutation (hereafter referred to as m.5541C > T cells). For comparison, we also established a cell line using mitochondria without this mutation (WT cells) ( 29 ). Besides our report ( 29 ), the m.5541C > T mutation has been identified in other studies as a causative factor for MELAS ( 55 , 56 ).

We first compared the abundance of hmtRNA Trp in m.5541C > T cells with that in WT cells by northern blotting. The level of mutant hmtRNA Trp was decreased by approximately 50%, whereas the levels of hmtRNA Lys and hmtRNA Leu (UUR) were not significantly different between the two cell lines (Figure 4A ). Subsequently, we directly monitored hmtRNA Trp τm 5 U modification content in the m.5541C > T cells. We purified hmtRNA Trp from WT and m. 5541C > T cells using biotin-labelled probes, digested it into mononucleosides and performed UPLC-MS/MS analyses. The results clearly showed that the τm 5 U level of hmtRNA Trp in cybrid cells was close to background and undetectable (Figure 4B ). In contrast, after purification of hmtRNA Leu (UUR) and hmtRNA Lys from the two cell lines, the τm 5 U level in hmtRNA Leu (UUR) or hmtRNA Lys in the m.5541C > T cells was comparable with that in WT cells, suggesting unaltered τm 5 U biogenesis capacity in the mutant cells (Figure 4C and Supplementary Figure S6A ). Consistently, the immunoblot results showed that both hGTPBP3 and hMTO1 exhibited similar abundance in the two cell lines ( Supplementary Figure S6B ).

Furthermore, we detected the abundance of representative components of the mitochondrial respiratory chain complex (RCC) encoded by both mtDNA and nuclear DNA (nDNA). In m.5541C > T cells, significantly lower levels of MT-ND4 (a Complex I subunit) and MT-COX2 (a Complex IV subunit) were observed; in contrast, the levels of MT-ND3 and MT-ND6 (two Complex I subunits) as well as MT-ATP6 and MT-ATP8 (two Complex V subunits) were unchanged in mutant cells when compared with WT cells (Figure 4D ). This suggests that tryptophan codon usage is not a limiting factor for the expression of these proteins in m.5541C > T cells, as MT-ATP8 (4.4%) contains higher tryptophan codon usage than MT-ND4 (2.8%) and MT-COX2 (1.8%). In parallel, the levels of nDNA-encoded NDUFS1 (a Complex I component) and COX4 (a Complex IV component) were also lower in mutant cells (Figure 4E ). Consistently, the assembly of the RCC complex, especially Complex I, was defective in m.5541C > T cells, as evidenced by blue native-PAGE (BN-PAGE) ( Supplementary Figure S6C ). Next, we performed OCR analyses. The results revealed decreased OCR activity in m.5541C > T cells. Consistently, basal respiration, maximal respiration and ATP production in m.5541C > T cells were significantly lower than in WT cells (Figure 4F ), showing that mitochondrial respiration was decreased by the m.5541C > T mutation.

Collectively, these results obtained with the patient-derived cybrid cell line reveal that the pathogenic m.5541C > T mutation abolishes τm 5 U biogenesis at the wobble position of hmtRNA Trp in vivo , contributing to the defects in mitochondrial translation and function observed in MELAS syndrome.

To better understand the impact of other pathogenic mtDNA mutations on the τm 5 U modification of hmtRNA Trp , we sought to introduce mtDNA mutations specifically in situ . Liu et al. designed a guide RNA-independent mtDNA editing tool termed DdCBE ( 57 ). DdCBE involves splitting the double-stranded DNA cytosine deaminase DddA tox domain (split-DddA tox ) and fusion with transcription activator-like effector (TALE) proteins and uracil glycosylase inhibitor to convert cytosine (C) to thymine (T) conversion at specific target sequences. Based on the editor’s preference and the sequence context of the hmtRNA Trp locus, mutations m.5532G > A and m.5545C > T in hmtRNA Trp were selected for the editing experiment ( Supplementary Figure S7A ).

Following a previous study, the editing efficiency of different split pairs at the target site was sequenced by Sanger sequencing to identify the most effective pairs ( 57 ). Subsequently, cells with edited mtDNA were selected for further cultivation via puromycin selection. Due to inherent variations in editing efficiencies among individual cells, the observed phenotype represents the average behavior of a mixed cell population. Flow cytometry was used to refine and homogenize this population, facilitating the isolation of individual cells. The isolated cells were subjected to extended cultivation with the explicit objective of attaining monoclonal purity and distinct editing efficiency. Sanger and high-throughput sequencing analyses conclusively demonstrated the successful derivation of cell lines, each manifesting divergent editing efficiencies and targeting positions m.5532G > A and m.5545C > T ( Supplementary Figure S7B and C ). We chose two cell lines among the highest editing efficiencies (with efficiencies of 90.98% and 86.75%) for the following assays, which are hereafter designated as m.5532G > A and m.5545C > T cell lines (Figure 5A and Supplementary Figure S7C ).

To explore whether the two mutations affected the abundance of hmtRNA Trp , we compared the steady-state levels of hmtRNA Trp and two other hmtRNAs, hmtRNA Lys and hmtRNA Leu (UUR), in the two mutants and a WT control cell line via northern blotting. Levels of hmtRNA Trp in m.5532G > A and m.5545C > T cell lines were decreased by approximately 50% compared with WT cells, and little effect was observed for hmtRNA Lys and hmtRNA Leu (UUR) (Figure 5B ). We isolated hmtRNA Trp and hmtRNA Lys from WT, m.5532G > A, and m.5545C > T cells and performed UPLC-MS/MS analyses. The level of τm 5 U in hmtRNA Trp in the m.5532G > A cells was reduced to background level, while that of m.5545C > T cells was detected, but with an obviously lower amount (Figure 5C ). However, τm 5 U abundance in hmtRNA Lys from both mutant cells was comparable with that in WT cells (noting that although τm 5 s 2 U is the predominant modification in hmtRNA Lys , the τm 5 s 2 U standard is not commercially available) (Figure 5D ). Both mutant cell lines contained similar levels of the τm 5 U-modifying enzymes, hGTPBP3 and hMTO1 ( Supplementary Figure S8A ). Taken together, these data clearly indicate that the m.5532G > A and m.5545C > T mutations substantially interfere with τm 5 U biogenesis in vivo .

The levels of mtDNA-encoded MT-COX2 were obviously lower in the m.5532G > A and m.5545C > T cell lines than in WT cells (Figure 5E ), which was consistent with the finding for m.5541C > T cells (Figure 4D ). Moreover, MT-ATP8 was significantly reduced in m.5545C > T cells, but not in m.5532G > A (Figure 5E ) and m.5541C > T cells (Figure 4D ). These findings suggested that MT-ATP8 production was not influenced by defective τm 5 U biogenesis, but was particularly sensitive to lack in a functional hmtRNA Trp , since the hmtRNA Trp m.5545C > T mutant was unable to efficiently recognize tryptophan codons due to mispairing between codon (UGA/G) and anticodon (U U A; the italicized U denotes the modified site) (Figure 3B ). In addition, the abundance of MT-ND6 was decreased in the two cybrid cells (Figure 5E ), which was different from m.5541C > T (Figure 4D ). As with m.5541C > T cells, the amount of MT-ATP6 was not significantly altered in the WT and two mutant cell types (Figure 5E ), suggesting that translation of MT-ATP6 mRNA was not impacted by the hmtRNA Trp τm 5 U modification defect. In addition, the level of NDUFS1 in the two mutant cell lines was significantly lower than that in WT cells and was more pronounced in m.5545C > T cells (Figure 5E ) . However, levels of nDNA-encoded SDHB (a Complex II subunit) and COX4 were not altered (Figure 5E ). Defective mitochondrial translation was confirmed by the disruption in the RCC complex assembly revealed by BN-PAGE. The gels displayed lower amounts of Complexes I and V, especially for m.5545C > T cells ( Supplementary Figure S8B ). To verify that the defective mitochondrial translation observed was caused by the desired point mutation induced by mitochondrial gene editing and not by other off-target mutations, we tested the protein content in edited cell lines harboring different editing efficiencies at position 5545. The abundance of nDNA-encoded NDUFS1 and mtDNA-encoded MT-ATP8 was negatively proportional to editing efficiency (mtDNA content); a lower mutation rate of m.5545C > T corresponded to a higher level of MT-ATP8 abundance ( Supplementary Figure S8C ).

We further examined the OCR activity of the mutant and control cells. The basal respiratory and maximal respiratory rates, proton leakage and ATP production of the two mutant cell lines were significantly lower than the values of WT cells (Figure 5F ). Impairment of respiratory activity was more pronounced in m.5545C > T cells (Figure 5F ), consistent with the reduced number of RCC components and their assembly (Figure 5E and Supplementary Figure S8B ).

Taken together, these data reveal a perturbation in mitochondrial energy metabolism and oxidative capacity in m.5532G > A and m.5545C > T cell lines. These mitochondrial tRNA editing experiments confirmed that D-stem (m.5532G > A) or anticodon loop (m.5545C > T) mutations prevent efficient τm 5 U modification of hmtRNA Trp in vivo , which impairs mitochondrial translation and function.

Taurine improves impaired mitochondrial function in patients with MELAS harboring the m.3243A > G variant in the hmtRNA Leu (UUR) locus and helps prevent stroke-like episodes ( 58 ). Given the above data demonstrating the τm 5 U modification defect of a wide range of hmtRNA Trp gene mutations, we aimed to understand whether taurine addition represents a similarly promising protective approach for hmtRNA Trp -related diseases. We chose the m.5541C > T cybrid cell as a model because it was constructed using patient-derived mitochondria. WT and m.5541C > T cells were supplemented with 40 mM taurine for 7 days. Northern blot analyses revealed that the steady-state level of hmtRNA Trp in the cybrid cells was significantly elevated in the presence of taurine, whereas the levels of hmtRNA Lys and hmtRNA Leu (UUR) did not change substantially (Figure 6A ). To investigate whether taurine supplementation could restore the τm 5 U modification, we isolated hmtRNA Trp from WT and m.5541C > T cells in the absence or presence of taurine addition. UPLC-MS/MS results revealed that, in comparison with the nearly eliminated τm 5 U level in hmtRNA Trp in untreated m.5541C > T cells, a small but detectable amount of τm 5 U in hmtRNA Trp was present in taurine-supplemented mutant cells (Figure 6B ). However, taurine treatment did not increase the τm 5 U level in hmtRNA Trp WT cells (Figure 6B ). Furthermore, the τm 5 U level in hmtRNA Lys in both cell lines was not increased by taurine supplementation (Figure 6B ). Consistently, hGTPBP3 and hMTO1 exhibited similar levels in WT and m.5541C > T cells with or without taurine supplementation ( Supplementary Figure S9A ). These data indicate that taurine supplementation to some extent enhances τm 5 U biogenesis in m.5541C > T cells and increases the steady-state level of hmtRNA Trp in mutant cells.

In addition, we detected the abundance of representative components of RCC complexes (mtDNA-encoded MT-ND4 and nDNA-encoded NDUFS1 and COX4), which exhibited significantly reduced levels in m.5541C > T cells (Figure 4D , E ). Remarkably, the levels of MT-ND4, NDUFS1 and COX4 were substantially restored by taurine supplementation (Figure 6C ). The mitochondrial translation that was meliorated by taurine supplementation was also observed by BN-PAGE, with an obviously increased amount of Complex I ( Supplementary Figure S9B ). However, RCC in the mutant cells with taurine addition still displayed lower levels than the levels in WT cells, indicating that taurine supplementation could not completely reverse mitochondrial functional defects ( Supplementary Figure S9B ).

Taken together, these results suggest that taurine supplementation results in increased hmtRNA Trp τm 5 U content and improves mitochondrial translation in patient-derived cells.
sections.discussion:
In this study, we purified a naturally assembled Ec MnmEG complex by gene coexpression and verified that it could modify all E. coli transcribed tRNA substrates in vitro , albeit with varying efficiencies, with the exception of Ec tRNA Gln (UUG). The lack of detectable modifications of Ec tRNA Gln (UUG) may be due to poor folding, slow catalytic efficiency or the absence of other modifications.

We demonstrated that Ec MnmEG is capable of introducing both cmnm 5 U and τm 5 U moiety to mitochondrial tRNA Trp , suggesting dual plasticity in amino acid and tRNA substrates. However, τm 5 U modification was only observed in the presence of a high concentration of taurine, indicating that the apparent binding affinity of Ec MnmEG for taurine is dramatically lower than that for Gly. Even though τm 5 U predominantly exists in mammalian mitochondria, a small fraction of mitochondrial tRNAs contain cmnm 5 U in physiological or stress conditions ( 6 , 11 ), suggesting hGTPBP3–hMTO1 is also inherently able to utilize Gly as a taurine substitute, but likely with a lower binding affinity. These observations indicate the existence of a conserved amino acid-binding pocket, a similar tRNA-recognition feature and a similar catalytic mechanism between MnmEG and hGTPBP3–hMTO1. Despite various structures of standalone MnmE and MnmG and a clear understanding of the recognition of numerous substrates or cofactors, including GTP and 5,10-CH 2 -THF accommodation by MnmE and FAD-binding by MnmG ( 9 , 45 , 59–62 ), the exact binding pocket and pattern for Gly or taurine in cmnm 5 U- or τm 5 U-modification remains unclear. In contrast, we found that all four hmtRNAs, except hmtRNA Trp , were not modified by Ec MnmEG. However, two hmtRNAs, hmtRNA Leu (UUR) and hmtRNA Lys , were efficiently charged by the corresponding aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases in previous studies ( 33 , 34 ). These findings suggest correct tRNA folding at aminoacylation level. Why these four hmtRNAs were not modified is unclear; it may be derived from inherently idiosyncratic features of hmtRNAs when compared with canonical tRNA structures ( 63 ), which are unfavorable for bacterial enzymes and/or lack of other modifications. The failure of modifying most τm 5 U-containing hmtRNAs makes it necessary to reconstitute the activity of the native or assembled hGTPBP3–hMTO1 complex for hmtRNAs in the future.

To date, over 900 pathogenic mutations have been mapped to mtDNA ( 64 , 65 ). Notably, mutations in hmtRNA loci account for approximately 40–50% of these disease-causing variants, in sharp contrast to the fact that hmtRNA genes occupy < 10% of the mtDNA content ( 66 ). This huge contrast highlights the crucial role of hmtRNAs in human health and diseases, and highlights the urgent need to clarify the molecular pathogenic mechanisms of hmtRNA-related diseases ( 63 , 65 , 67 ). Through in vitro activity reconstitution and in vivo assessment of τm 5 U-modification abundance in both a patient-derived cell line and two mtDNA editing HEK293FT cell lines, it was demonstrated that all mutations occurring in the anticodon stem, loop and D-stem regions significantly impaired τm 5 U-biogenesis in hmtRNA Trp . Notably, an SNP in the T-loop of hmtRNA Trp did not substantially influence U34 modification in vitro . These findings emphasize the importance of the anticodon stem, loop and D-stem regions in recognition, likely jointly mediated by FAD binding, Ins-2 and helical domains in MnmG/MTO1 ( 61 ). In this regard, cmnm 5 U- or τm 5 U-modifying enzymes seem to bind the double helix domain in the L-shaped tRNA three-dimensional structure, comprising of D-stem/loop and anticodon stem/loop. This finding may offer insight into understanding the elimination of τm 5 U formation due to m. 3243A > G, m.3244G > A, m.3258T > C and m.3271T > C mutations in the hmtRNA Leu (UUR) locus ( 28 ). However, m.8344A > G in the hmtRNA Lys mutation is located in the T-loop; the reason for the resultant loss of τm 5 U modification remains unclear ( 68 ). Considering that hmtRNA Lys is a tRNA that is highly dependent on modification for structural stabilization ( 32 ) and that m.8344A > G abolishes N 1 -methyladenosine modification at base 58 (m 1 A58) ( 69 ), which is a crucial architecture-stabilizing modification ( 70 ), we hypothesize that m.8344A > G impairs recognition by hGTPBP3–hMTO1 due to an alternative conformation. hmtRNA Trp is unique among all hmtRNAs because it contains a natural A29-C41 mismatch (m.A5539-m.C5551) in the anticodon stem ( 35 ). An identical A29-C41 mismatch (m.A15914-m. C15926 ) is also present in hmtRNA Thr ( 35 ). We have proven that the presence of this mismatch makes nucleotides in the anticodon stem of hmtRNA Thr particularly susceptible to local mutations, which would otherwise disrupt the double helix anticodon stem structure into single strands and influence the aminoacylation and modification of the anticodon loop ( 35 ). In parallel, we suggest that one of the reasons for pathogenic mutations concentrating in the anticodon stem of hmtRNA Trp is the existence of an A29-C41 mismatch. Notably, despite the τm 5 U modification defect induced by hmtRNA Trp mutations, we propose that this defect is only one of multiple tRNA metabolism defects. Indeed, m.5545C > T likely decreases hmtRNA Trp aminoacylation levels due to its reliance on anticodon recognition by TrpRS ( 71 , 72 ). Moreover, we observed a lower abundance of hmtRNA Trp in patient-derived and edited cell lines. The reduced number of hmtRNA Trp mutants was likely not derived from disruptive mtDNA transcription, because the abundance of other hmtRNAs from the same mtDNA strand (H-strand), such as hmtRNA Leu (UUR) and hmtRNA Lys ( 63 , 66 ), remained unaltered. Loss of τm 5 U modification in hmtRNA Trp may trigger a tRNA quality control mechanism in mitochondria. Accordingly, after taurine supplementation, increased τm 5 U modification was accompanied by elevated hmtRNA Trp levels. The detailed relationship between U34 modifications and hmtRNA Trp levels remains unclear. Our work provides the third example of hmtRNA mutation-related τm 5 U-hypomodification among the five τm 5 U-harboring tRNAs. Whether some variants in hmtRNA Glu and hmtRNA Gln , especially those in the anticodon stem and loop regions ( 30 , 31 , 54 ), also impact τm 5 U modification requires further study. Functionally, τm 5 U formation restricts tRNA decoding spectrum for split box codons and promotes tRNA decoding efficiency for cognate codons ( 14 , 15 ). Given the loss of τm 5 U modification in m.5541C > T cells, we tried to search for any misrecognition of UGY (Y = U, C) Cys codons. We failed to identify Cys-to-Trp misincorporation in the mtDNA-encoded peptides, implying that τm 5 U-hypomodification in hmtRNA Trp is not important in translational fidelity. The biological role of hmtRNA Trp τm 5 U modification in cognate codon reading remains to be determined.

Currently, there are no therapeutic drugs and strategies for treating mitochondrial diseases. The amino acid analog taurine is involved in various biological functions ( 73 , 74 ). In mammalian cells, taurine accumulates from cysteine de novo through cysteine sulfonic acid decarboxylase or the diet ( 73 ). The abundance of taurine decreases with age, and infants have low de novo taurine synthesis activity ( 74 ). Therefore, dietary taurine is essential for normal development. Phase III clinical trial data of oral supplementation of taurine ( 58 , 75 ) show that it can effectively relieve symptoms by increasing the modification level of the MELAS-associated mutant hmtRNA Leu (UUR). Similarly, we provide evidence that taurine supplementation increases the level of hmtRNA Trp in m.5541C > T mutant cells, accompanied by an increase in mitochondrial translation. We suggest that the catalytic efficiency of hGTPBP3–hMTO1 is likely elevated at higher taurine concentrations to promote τm 5 U modification, which subsequently makes the hmtRNA Trp mutant more active in the translation cycle and concurrently less accessible to tRNA quality control pathway for degradation. Taurine supplementation as a potential intervention strategy should be further explored in animal models of hmtRNA Trp -related diseases.
